content: Globally, there has been a substantial increase in HIV testing services (HTS). In 2005, only 10% of people with HIV in Africa were aware of their status, and globally, only 12% of individuals who wanted to test for HIV could do so. By contrast, nearly 15 years later, 81% of people with HIV in Africa and 79% globally are estimated to know their status. Between 2010 and 2018, over one billion people received HTS in lowand middle-income countries, largely due to the availability of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs). These tests have enabled task-sharing, allowing trained lay providers to deliver HTS in non-laboratory settings, including health facilities and community outreach programs. Despite these achievements, significant gaps in testing remain. Many individuals at the highest risk of HIV, such as men, adolescents (ages 10–19), young people (ages 15–24), and key populations in high-burden areas like East and Southern Africa, remain untested. Key populations disproportionately affected by HIV include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, and incarcerated individuals. Although many countries have prioritized these populations in their national HTS guidelines, implementation remains limited, and coverage is low. Barriers include inaccessible and unacceptable services, stigma, discrimination, and punitive laws. These challenges hinder access to HIV prevention, testing, treatment, and care. Men with HIV are less likely than women to know their status, receive treatment, or achieve viral suppression. In 2018, only 55% of adult men with HIV were receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), compared to 68% of women. Men are overrepresented in key populations and face additional barriers, such as stigma, confidentiality concerns, and inconvenient clinic hours. These factors contribute to delayed diagnosis and treatment, resulting in higher HIV-related mortality rates among men compared to women. Adolescents and young people, particularly young women and girls in high-burden settings, are also underserved. In sub-Saharan Africa, fewer than one in five girls aged 15–19 are aware of their HIV status. Population-based surveys in countries like Malawi, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia suggest that only about half of young people aged 15–24 with HIV know their status, and only 37–46% are on treatment. Barriers include restrictive laws, such as age-of-consent requirements for testing, and poor-quality services. Efforts are needed to improve access to HTS for adolescents in high-incidence areas and young key populations globally. HIV testing coverage among children is also low. Although early infant diagnosis (EID) rates have improved, only 56% of HIV-exposed infants were tested by two months of age in 2018. Delays in obtaining results and linking infants to care persist, with less than one-third of perinatally infected infants initiating ART in a timely manner. Linkage to prevention, care, and treatment following HTS is critical but often delayed. While ART access has improved, gaps remain, particularly for key populations, men, and young people. Barriers include transportation costs, stigma, and long clinic wait times. Testing strategies that rely on laboratory-based methods, such as Western blotting, result in longer turnaround times and lower linkage rates compared to simpler methods like RDTs. Innovative, people-centered approaches are needed to improve linkage to care and address these challenges. Misdiagnosis can occur due to suboptimal testing algorithms, poor product performance, and user errors. Only 25% of countries have HIV testing strategies fully aligned with WHO recommendations. QA systems must expand alongside HTS delivery to prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary treatment initiation. The WHO’s 2019 consolidated guidelines on HTS aim to address these gaps by providing evidence-based recommendations and operational guidance. These guidelines emphasize the importance of reaching underserved populations, integrating services, and ensuring quality testing. They also highlight the need for a public health and human rights-based approach, prioritizing universal health coverage, gender equality, and accessibility. The guidelines advocate for adherence to the WHO’s 5 Cs—Consent, Confidentiality, Counseling, Correct test results, and Connection to care and treatment.
